lead: A bar under load does not feel force at a point; it spreads that force over an area. Stress is the spread: internal force divided by the area of the face it acts on. When the force is perpendicular to the face you get normal stress, in tension or compression. When the force slides along the face you get shear stress, the kind that slices a rivet or punches a hole. Every strength check — a tie rod, a bolt, a hoarding's anchor in a Chennai cyclone — begins with these two numbers.

sections.h3: Cut the bar and look at the internal force

blocks.text: A rigid body is a bookkeeping idea: it never bends, so forces only balance. Real members bend and break, so we must look inside. Take a 20 mm steel rod carrying 50 kN in tension. Imagine a saw cut straight across it. The two halves still pull on each other with 50 kN, because the rod was in balance before the cut. That pull, spread over the cut face, is what the material feels.
Normal stress is the internal force perpendicular to the cut, per unit area.

blocks.where: σ is the normal stress in N/m² (Pa); P is the axial force normal to the cut in N; A is the cross-section area in m².

blocks.text: The pascal is small: 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Steel works at millions of pascals, so engineers use 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa. Also 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², so a value in N/mm² equals the same value in MPa.

The sign is a convention, not a size. Plus means tension: the force pulls away from the cut face and the bar gets longer. Minus means compression: the force pushes into the face and the bar gets shorter. Always write it. A compressive 159 MPa is a different design case from a tensile 159 MPa.
Stress is not force. Halve the area and the same 50 kN doubles the stress. A thin wire and a thick rod can carry the same load, but the wire sits closer to breaking.

sections.h3: Shear stress acts along the face

blocks.text: Shear stress acts along the cut face, not across it. Two plates joined by a 20 mm rivet and pulled apart slice the rivet at the joint plane. The force on that plane is V, the shear force.

blocks.where: τ is the average shear stress in N/m² (Pa); V is the shear force along the face in N; A_s is the area carrying the shear in m².

blocks.text: For a rivet in single shear, A_s is the rivet cross-section, πd²/4. If the rivet has two cut planes it is in double shear: A_s = 2 × πd²/4, and each plane carries V/2. Miss this and the answer is out by a factor of two.

Punching works the same way. A 20 mm punch through a 10 mm plate shears out a plug; the sheared surface is a cylinder of area πdt = π × 20 mm × 10 mm = 628.3 mm². With 150 kN of punch force, τ = 150 000 N / 628.3 mm² = 238.7 N/mm². Shops check punch capacity exactly this way.

V/A_s gives an average. The real shear stress on a solid circular rivet section is zero at the top and bottom of the section and reaches 4V/(3A) at the centre — one-third above the average. Simple design uses the average V/A_s. Some syllabi call normal stress direct stress and shear stress tangential stress. Same quantities.

items: Find the force on the member from a free body diagram, in N.
Decide which face is cut and whether the force is across it (normal) or along it (shear).
Take the matching area: cross-section for tension or compression, shear plane for shear, in m² or mm².
Divide, keep the units consistent, and attach the sign for normal stress.

blocks.text: Judge the size. Mild steel yields near 250 N/mm², so 159 MPa is about two-thirds of yield — working, but not generous. Aluminium is not automatically weaker: many wrought alloys have yield strengths of 200 MPa or more, while some cast grades are far weaker. Never assume a strength; take the value for the actual alloy from a table. A stress means little until you compare it with the material's strength (see 1.2). The rod also stretches, and that uses the same P and A (see 1.6).

figure.caption: The upper path turns the 50 kN axial load into normal stress by dividing by the rod's 314.2 mm² cross-section; the dashed path turns a shear force into shear stress on the cut plane. The cut is the decision point: everything after it depends on which face you took.

spec.title: From load to stress
spec.aria: An axial load is cut to expose an internal force, which gives normal stress; a shear force on a face gives shear stress.

examples.question: A 20 mm diameter steel rod carries an axial tensile load of 50 kN. Find the normal stress in the rod.
steps: Given: diameter d = 20 mm, tensile load P = 50 kN = 50 000 N.
Normal stress σ = P/A = 50 000 N / 314.16 mm² = 159.16 N/mm².
Convert: 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa, so σ = 159.2 MPa, positive because the load is tensile.
examples.answer: The rod carries a tensile normal stress of 159.2 MPa (159.2 N/mm²).
examples.check:
import math
d = 20.0
P = 50000.0
A = math.pi * d**2 / 4
sigma = P / A
print(f"{A:.1f}")
print(f"{sigma:.1f}")

traps: Using the diameter as the radius: the area is πd²/4, never πd².
Mixing mm² and m²: 1 m² = 10⁶ mm², and 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa = 10⁶ N/m².
Taking the full cross-section as the shear area: shear acts on the cut plane, πdt for a punched hole, twice the section for double shear.
Dropping the sign: + for tension, − for compression; an unsigned compression answer loses marks.
Stress is force per area; an answer in kN is a force, not a stress, and scores zero however right the number looks.

quiz.q: Define normal stress and state its SI unit.
quiz.a: Normal stress is the internal force perpendicular to a cut face divided by the area of that face, σ = P/A. Unit: N/m², called the pascal (Pa); in practice N/mm² or MPa.

quiz.q: What does a negative value of σ mean?
quiz.a: The member is in compression: the internal force pushes into the cut face and the bar shortens.

quiz.q: Why is stress a better design number than force?
quiz.a: The same force on a smaller area gives a higher stress and a greater chance of failure. Stress normalises force by area, so it can be compared directly with the material's yield or ultimate strength, which are themselves measured as stresses.

quiz.q: A rivet joins three plates and is loaded so that two cut planes carry the load. How does A_s differ from that of a rivet in single shear?
quiz.a: In double shear the load is shared by two planes, so A_s = 2 × πd²/4. Each plane carries V/2 and the average shear stress is V/(2πd²/4), half the single-shear value for the same V.

quiz.q: A 16 mm diameter rod carries 40 kN in tension. Find the normal stress.
A 25 mm punch makes a hole in an 8 mm plate under 200 kN. Find the average shear stress in the plate.
Two rods of the same material carry the same 50 kN. Rod A is 20 mm diameter, rod B is 40 mm. Compare their stresses and say which is nearer to yielding, with numbers.
quiz.a: A_A = 314.2 mm², σ_A = 159.2 MPa; A_B = 1256.6 mm², σ_B = 39.8 MPa. Rod A has four times the stress because doubling the diameter quadruples the area. Against a 250 MPa yield, rod A uses 64% of its strength and rod B only 16%, so rod A yields first.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real parts the stress at a hole or a shoulder is several times the average, and a stress concentration factor K_t corrects for it. Wheel-on-rail and ball-bearing contacts are governed by Hertzian contact stress, which is a normal stress on a curved surface. Finite element software draws pictures of exactly these two quantities, and a designer reads peak von Mises stress, not force. When several stresses act on the same point, they combine into principal stresses, which is where Unit 2 begins. Search next for stress concentration factor, Hertzian contact stress, and von Mises stress.
